title: Event 1 - AWS VIETNAM COMMUNITY MEETUP
content:
AWS VIETNAM COMMUNITY MEETUP Event Information Item Details Event Name AWS VIETNAM COMMUNITY MEETUP Date Saturday, July 25, 2026 Time 08:30 – 12:00 (GMT+7) Location AWS Hanoi – 7th Floor, Grand Terra Tower, 36 Cat Linh Street, Dong Da District, Hanoi Role Attendee Summary Report Event Objectives AI is changing the way we build products, grow businesses, and solve real-world problems. Are you ready to explore the latest AI trends and how to apply them on AWS?
Join the AWS Vietnam Community Meetup to meet AWS Community Heroes, Community Builders, and experts who are directly implementing AI in businesses.
Speakers Ho Viet Anh Tuan Vu Nguyen Thu Nam La Duc Bui Key Highlights OpenClaw – The Rise and Practice of Open-Source AI Agents What OpenClaw actually is - an open-source agent runtime The OpenClaw layered architecture (L1–L4) Real-world use cases and advanced multi-agent capabilities Where things start to break What this means for developers AI Trends Through the Lens of an Infrastructure Engineer Setting the scene: How AI is reshaping infrastructure How AI has changed the Infrastructure Engineer’s job AI across the infrastructure stack: IaC, AIOps, FinOps, Security, GenAI coding What’s next: agentic and AI-native infrastructure Skills and challenges ahead Community Update These are memorable milestones that have shaped the community’s development over the years. Knowledge-sharing activities during meetings. Collaborate and work with AWS in the US. Ship Fast with AI, Not by Encode knowledge as infrastructure Build a shared language with your agents Keep your docs inside the repo Critical code? Write more code Build a superpowered engineer From AI Trends to Business Value How has AI helped Sales create business value? What do sales spend their time on? AI support is provided at every stage AI doesn’t close deals. People do Key Takeaways 1. Ship Fast with AI, Not by AI Inner Loop — The write → run → debug cycle. AI has already made this ~10x faster. Outer Loop — Review → integrate → deploy → operate. Still entirely human-paced; nothing speeds it up automatically. Encode Knowledge as Infrastructure — Turn recurring issues into lint rules or CI checks that block them permanently, instead of fixing the same thing by hand every time. Living Wiki — A shared markdown “language” between humans and agents — agents read it before naming things and write to it when a new concept crystallizes. Stay the Author — The goal isn’t a superpowered agent, it’s a superpowered engineer — the human stays the one accountable for the work. 2. AI Trends – Infrastructure Engineer AIOps — AI automatically detects anomalies and predicts infrastructure incidents before they impact users. AI-driven IaC — AI generates infrastructure code (Terraform/CDK) from plain-language prompts, reviews it, and flags configuration drift. FinOps — AI continuously analyzes usage to optimize cost in real time (right-sizing, Savings Plan recommendations). Agentic Infrastructure — The maturity curve infrastructure is climbing: Assisted → Automated → Agentic → Self-managing. Explainability — Understanding why AI made a decision — a requirement for trusting it and staying accountable for it. 3. AI Trends to Business – Sales AI / GenAI / Agent — The three layers of AI technology Sales teams are adopting, from simple assistants to autonomous agents. Time Allocation Gap — Sales reps spend only 5–10% of their time actually meeting customers; the rest is repetitive prep work. AI-Augmented Sales Journey — AI supports every stage: prospecting → research → discovery → proposal → follow-up. Time-to-Value Compression — AI drastically shortens tasks like research and proposal writing (e.g., research from 2 hours down to 20 minutes). Human Trust — Trust, relationships, communication, and negotiation remain things AI cannot replace when closing a deal. 4. OpenClaw – Open-Source AI Agents Agent Runtime — OpenClaw isn’t an app; it’s an “operating system” for running and hosting AI agents. Layered Architecture (L1–L4) — From the model-calling layer (L1) to the agent execution loop (L2), the coding-agent layer (L3), and the gateway with memory/cron/sessions (L4). Agent Loop (Steering + Follow-ups) — The mechanism that lets an agent reason, call tools, and decide its next action on its own. Skill Injection Risk — A security risk where an agent’s skills/plugins can contain malicious code or be exploited via prompt injection. Memory as Prompt Augmentation — What’s currently called agent “memory” is really just extra text injected into the prompt, not true structured memory. Event Experience Attending the AWS Vietnam Community Meetup was a valuable experience during my AI and cloud learning journey. The event brought together several technical sharing sessions covering both infrastructure and business applications of AI.
I particularly enjoyed the “OpenClaw” presentation because it demonstrated how an open-source project could grow from a simple WhatsApp relay bot into a full agent runtime that surpassed React in GitHub stars within just a few months. The “Ship Fast with AI, Not by AI” talk also inspired me by showing that writing code faster with AI isn’t enough — real speed comes from investing in review, testing, and shared knowledge across a team.
Besides technical talks, the session on AI trends from an infrastructure engineer’s perspective helped me understand how AIOps, FinOps, and AI-driven IaC are reshaping day-to-day cloud operations. I also found the sales-focused talk on empowering business with AI insightful, as it showed how AI can free up professionals from repetitive prep work to focus on building real customer relationships.
Overall, the event gave me the opportunity to interact with cloud and AI professionals, exchange ideas with other participants, and better understand where the industry is heading — from AI-assisted coding to fully agentic infrastructure.
Lessons Learned This event taught me that AI’s biggest impact isn’t just making individual tasks faster — it’s about rethinking how work gets structured around AI. From “Ship Fast with AI, Not by AI,” I learned that writing code faster is meaningless if review, testing, and deployment don’t scale with it; real productivity comes from investing in shared infrastructure like lint rules and living documentation, not just the AI-generated output itself.
The infrastructure talk showed me that AI adoption in cloud engineering isn’t just about automation — it’s a shift in role, from manually operating systems to designing and supervising ones that increasingly manage themselves. This also comes with new responsibilities, especially around explainability and security, since trusting an AI decision requires understanding why it was made.
From the OpenClaw session, I learned that as agents gain more autonomy and tool access, their capabilities are scaling faster than the safety guardrails around them — a reminder that “memory” and “permissions” in AI agents still need much more rigorous design than they currently have.
Finally, the sales-focused talk reinforced an important balance: AI is excellent at removing repetitive work, but trust, relationships, and negotiation still depend entirely on people. Overall, this event helped me see AI not as a replacement for skill or judgment, but as a tool that only creates real value when paired with strong human oversight and well-designed systems around it.

title: Worklog
content:
This section summarizes my internship progress over 12 weeks. Throughout the internship, I followed a structured learning roadmap that started with AWS fundamental services and gradually advanced to designing, developing, deploying, and operating a complete cloud-based application.
During the first eight weeks, I focused on learning AWS core services such as IAM, EC2, VPC, Amazon S3, Amazon RDS, Security Groups, Network ACLs, Amazon Route 53, Application Load Balancer, Amazon CloudWatch, Docker, Amazon ECS, and CI/CD concepts. These activities provided the technical foundation required for the internship project.
From Week 9 onward, I began preparing the internship project by researching technologies, designing the system architecture, developing the application, and finally deploying the complete solution on AWS Cloud.
The internship project, TechMarket E-Commerce Platform, was successfully developed and deployed using Amazon ECS Fargate, Amazon ECR, Amazon S3, MongoDB Atlas, Application Load Balancer, Amazon Route 53, AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), Amazon CloudWatch, and AWS CodeBuild.
The weekly worklog is organized as follows:
Week 1: AWS Fundamentals: Account Setup, IAM Security, Budgets & Support Plans
